props.title: Bombay
props.initialSlug: Love defies religious riots in 1990s Bombay

sections.content: Mani Ratnam's Bombay (1995) stands as a pivotal work in Indian cinema, confronting Hindu-Muslim tensions through an interfaith love story set against the backdrop of the 1992-93 Bombay riots. The film broke new ground with A.R. Rahman's groundbreaking soundtrack and cinematographer Rajiv Menon's raw, documentary-style footage of riot sequences. It follows directly from Ratnam's terrorism trilogy, starting with Roja (1992) and including Dil Se (1998), establishing his mastery of politically charged romantic drama. The film's impact was so significant it faced censorship challenges and threats, yet went on to influence how Indian cinema handles communal subjects.

sections.content: The mid-1990s marked a crucial shift in Indian cinema's approach to political subjects. While Bombay tackled communal harmony head-on, films like Earth (1998) revisited partition trauma, and Mission Kashmir (2000) explored terrorism through a more commercial lens. Ratnam's influence sparked a wave of socially conscious mainstream films that didn't shy away from controversial subjects while maintaining commercial appeal. This period also saw the rise of parallel cinema addressing similar themes, like Govind Nihalani's Tamas (1988).

The film's technical innovations were equally revolutionary. Rahman's fusion score, blending Qawwali with contemporary orchestration, set new standards for Indian film music. The riot sequences, shot with handheld cameras and natural lighting, influenced later films like Black Friday (2004) and Parzania (2007). Ratnam's decision to cast Manisha Koirala and Arvind Swami - stars from different film industries - highlighted the pan-Indian scope of the story. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Indian Cinema

sections.content: Bombay's DNA can be traced in contemporary films like Mulk (2018) and Article 15 (2019), which tackle religious and caste discrimination respectively. The film's influence extends beyond subject matter to visual grammar - the way Gully Boy (2019) captures Mumbai's streets or Rang De Basanti (2006) portrays youth activism shows clear lineage to Ratnam's groundbreaking work.
